rationale: The BOOK ENTRY makes three material assertions: (1) Nineveh is a 'great city of the sea,' (2) it stands for Gentile people who repent, and (3) those people rise in judgment against those who reject Jesus. Assertions (2) and (3) are carried almost verbatim by the single printed reference, Matthew 12:41 ('The men of Nineveh shall rise in judgment with this generation, and shall condemn it: because they repented...'), with the generalization from 'this generation' to 'those who reject Jesus' warranted by the immediate context (the generation that demanded a sign and refused the greater-than-Jonah). Assertion (1) is a symbolic modifier, and the supporting chapter supplies its mechanics: Jonah repeatedly titles Nineveh 'that great city' (Jonah 1:2; 3:2; 4:11), and the sea is a scripturally defined symbol for peoples, multitudes, and nations (Revelation 17:15), so 'city of the sea' = a great mass of Gentile peoples — exactly what the second clause of the entry says. Since Nineveh was not literally a maritime city, the symbolic reading is the only coherent one, and it is internally consistent with the entry's own gloss. The strongest counter — the standard dual reading of Nineveh as both the repentant pagan city of Jonah and the wicked empire judged in Nahum — is broader than the entry but does not contradict its core: the repentance/rise-in-judgment strand is common to both, and Jesus' own use in Matthew 12:41 (the only text the entry prints) is precisely the strand the entry defines. A glossary entry scoped to the Sign of Jonah chapter is not defeated by the existence of an additional Nahum motif it does not address. No supplied text is better explained by the counter in a way the entry's identification cannot accommodate.
book_core_identification: Nineveh symbolizes the Gentile peoples (a 'great city' of the sea of nations) who repented at the preaching of Jonah and who will rise in judgment to condemn those who reject Jesus, per Matthew 12:41.
book_secondary_elaborations: Nineveh is titled a 'great city' (echoing Jonah 1:2; 3:2; 4:11).
The city is 'of the sea,' i.e., composed of the sea of peoples/nations (sea = peoples per Revelation 17:15).
The Ninevites' rising is specifically 'in judgment against those who reject Jesus,' generalizing Matthew 12:41's 'this generation.'
chapter_only_objections: The claim that 'the heart of the earth' is Jerusalem rather than the tomb is a contested chapter argument, not asserted in the glossary entry.
The reading of anastēsontai in Matthew 12:41 as literal bodily resurrection of the Ninevites (rather than a courtroom idiom) is a chapter-level inference.
The identification of the great fish with Caesar/Rome and the scene-by-scene Passion typology of Jonah 1–2 are chapter claims outside the entry.
The 'three days' journey = three thousand years' calculation via 2 Peter 3:8 is a speculative chapter claim.
Linking Nineveh's title 'that great city' to Revelation's harlot title (Rev 17:18; 18:21) is a chapter-level association not printed in the entry.
strongest_counter_interpretation: Nineveh is the historical Assyrian capital functioning as a dual biblical symbol: primarily the great pagan city that repented at Jonah's preaching and received God's mercy (Jonah 3; Matt 12:41), and secondarily the violent, arrogant imperial 'bloody city' destroyed under divine judgment (Nahum 1–3; Zephaniah 2:13-15) — with no symbolic 'sea' component, since Nineveh sat on the Tigris, not the sea.
counter_core_identification: Nineveh = the wicked pagan city/empire that both exemplifies repentance and mercy (Jonah/Gospels) and stands under certain divine judgment (Nahum/Zephaniah).
material_core_denial: The counter does not deny the entry's core; it affirms that the Ninevites are repentant Gentiles who will rise in judgment against Jesus' unrepentant generation (Matt 12:41) and merely adds a second motif (Nahum's judgment oracle) that the entry, scoped to the Sign of Jonah, does not address. Its only pointed disagreement is with the 'of the sea' modifier, which it would call geographically inaccurate rather than symbolically defined.
counter_case: Matthew 12:41 and Luke 11:32 support the repentance/judgment reading equally well without any 'sea' symbolism.
Nahum 1–3 and Zephaniah 2:13-15 show Nineveh's dominant Old Testament role as the judged bloody city, which the entry omits.
Historically Nineveh was an inland city on the Tigris, so 'city of the sea' is not literally true and requires an extra symbolic step.
The common reading requires no chained symbol definitions, only the plain sense of the cited texts.
book_explanatory_advantages: The entry's core is a near-quotation of the only printed reference, Matthew 12:41, so its central identification has direct textual carriage.

The 'of the sea' modifier is not free-floating: Revelation 17:15 explicitly defines waters as 'peoples, and multitudes, and nations,' and Jonah's own mirrored phrase 'heart of the seas' (Jonah 2:3) embeds the sea-of-nations symbolism inside the very book that features Nineveh.

The entry explains why Jesus selects Nineveh as the exemplar: as the great Gentile mass that turned at the preaching of a man given back from the deep, it prefigures the nations' response to the risen Lord — coherently tying Matt 12:41's 'rise in judgment' to the repentant-Gentile identity.
'That great city' (Jonah 1:2; 3:2; 4:11) supports the 'great city' wording of the entry verbatim.
counter_explanatory_advantages: The counter accounts for the Nahum/Zephaniah judgment strand, which the entry does not mention.
It avoids the symbolic step required to call an inland Tigris city a 'city of the sea.'
decisive_sources: Matthew 12:41 (KJV excerpt: the men of Nineveh repented and shall rise in judgment and condemn this generation)
Revelation 17:15 (waters = peoples, multitudes, nations — the defined symbol behind 'of the sea')
Luke 11:30-32 (Jonah himself a sign to the Ninevites; repentant Gentiles contrasted with the unbelieving generation)
unresolved_objections: The entry silently omits Nineveh's equally canonical role as the judged 'bloody city' of Nahum; as a general-purpose definition this is incomplete, though as a scoped symbolic gloss keyed to Matthew 12:41 it is accurate.

The sea = peoples symbol is asserted here on Revelation 17:15 with the full case study deferred to a later part of the book, so the 'of the sea' modifier rests on a definition proven elsewhere rather than in the supplied excerpts.
